prayer.text: Holy Spirit, protector of the Church, guide us into all truth.

cues.text: Chalcedon's Unfinished Business
A century after Chalcedon, the schism between the council's supporters and the Monophysite churches that rejected it still threatened the unity of the Eastern Roman Empire.
Emperor Justinian I devoted enormous energy throughout his long reign to restoring both imperial and religious unity.
He was determined to reconcile the Monophysites without repudiating Chalcedon itself.
He looked for a way to show that Chalcedon had never been friendly to Nestorianism — the very charge Monophysites leveled against it.
Justinian settled on a target: three theologians whose writings, decades earlier, had leaned toward language later associated with Nestorius.
None had themselves been condemned by name at Chalcedon, and one, Ibas, had actually been personally rehabilitated by that council.
These came to be called the "Three Chapters" : the person and writings of Theodore of Mopsuestia , certain writings of Theodoret of Cyrus , and a letter attributed to Ibas of Edessa .
In 543 or 544, Justinian issued an edict condemning all three.
A Reluctant Pope

Western bishops, especially in Africa and Italy, resisted the edict, fearing that condemning writers whom Chalcedon itself had not censured would appear to undermine that council's authority and hand the Monophysites a symbolic victory.

Pope Vigilius , brought to Constantinople under imperial pressure in 547, spent years resisting, then partially yielding to, then withdrawing his agreement from Justinian's condemnation, a wavering that badly damaged his standing in the West.
To settle the matter conclusively, Justinian summoned a general council to meet at Constantinople in 553.
Vigilius, still in the city but unwilling to preside over a council he suspected of being stacked against him, declined to attend in person, though he continued negotiating from a distance.
The Council's Verdict

The council opened on May 5, 553 under the presidency of Patriarch Eutychius of Constantinople , attended overwhelmingly by Eastern bishops; only a handful of Western, chiefly African, bishops were present.
Over eight sessions, the bishops examined writings attributed to Theodore, Theodoret, and Ibas.
On June 2, 553 , they formally condemned the Three Chapters in fourteen anathemas, while explicitly reaffirming Chalcedon and the first three ecumenical councils.
The council also condemned a set of propositions attributed to the theologian Origen , addressing a separate controversy over Origenist teaching that had been unsettling monasteries in Palestine.
Vigilius's Reversal
Justinian struck the pope's name from the diptychs and, by some accounts, had Vigilius's household exiled.

This pressure finally brought the pope to submission after eight years, on and off, of detention in Constantinople—one of the longest and most humiliating ordeals any pope endured at the hands of a Christian emperor.
In December 553, in a letter to Patriarch Eutychius, and again in a formal Constitutum the following February, Vigilius accepted the council's condemnation of the Three Chapters.
He compared his change of mind to St. Augustine's willingness to correct his own earlier writings, rather than presenting it as mere capitulation to force.
Even so, the council's reception in the West was troubled.
Several northern Italian provinces, including Milan and Aquileia , broke communion with Rome over what became known as the Schism of the Three Chapters .
They were convinced that condemning writers Chalcedon itself had not censured set a dangerous precedent for revisiting settled conciliar judgments.
Aquileia's bishops did not return to communion with Rome for well over a century, one of the longest-running internal ruptures in the early medieval Western Church.
Legacy
Constantinople II is counted as the fifth ecumenical council, though its narrow theological target—writers, not living heresies—has made it least remembered outside specialist study.

It produced no new creed comparable to those of Nicaea or Constantinople I. Its lasting significance lies less in new doctrine than in its formal ratification of the first four councils as an authoritative body of teaching.
It also demonstrated how deeply the fault lines opened at Chalcedon still ran through the Church a hundred years later.
Justinian's underlying hope was ultimately disappointed: condemning the Three Chapters did not draw the Monophysite churches back into communion with Constantinople and Rome.
The Monophysite churches remained separated, while the council's own reception cost the West dearly in internal unity.
The episode stands as a caution, echoed at several later points in Church history, about how far doctrinal precision pursued for the sake of reconciliation can end up producing new division instead.
